domains.title: Circuit Theory
domains.blurb: The electrical laws every lab is built on.

nodes.name: Ohm's Law & Power
nodes.title: What is Ohm's Law, and how does power follow from it
nodes.summary: V = I·R and the power it implies.

sections.heading: The fundamental relationship
sections.body: Voltage, current and resistance are locked together by V = I·R. Rearranged, it sizes a current-limiting resistor, predicts the voltage across a sensor, or confirms a wire can carry the load. Dividers, bridges and amplifier gain are all this law applied repeatedly.

sections.heading: Power dissipation
sections.body: Power is P = V·I = I²·R. A resistor turns electrical energy into heat; exceed its rating and it browns, smells, and drifts. Assume 1/4 W resistors on the bench and check I²R before powering anything that draws real current.

nodes.hint: A resistor getting hot or smelling burnt means you exceeded its 1/4 W rating — compute I²R, then raise the resistance or use a higher-wattage part before re-testing.

nodes.name: Voltage Divider Rule
nodes.title: How does a voltage divider turn resistance into a readable voltage
nodes.summary: Reading resistive sensors as a voltage.

sections.heading: Splitting a voltage
sections.body: Two series resistors split the supply: Vout = Vin · R2 / (R1 + R2). Almost every resistive sensor here — the LDR, the thermistor, the soil probe — is read by making it one leg of a divider and watching how Vout moves as its resistance changes.

sections.heading: Choosing the fixed resistor
sections.body: Pick the fixed resistor near the sensor's mid-range resistance so the output swings across the widest part of the ADC range. A poor choice squashes your signal into a handful of counts.

nodes.hint: An ADC reading pinned at 0 or 1023 means the fixed resistor is mismatched to the sensor — measure the sensor at both extremes and choose a fixed resistor in between.

nodes.name: Pull-up / Pull-down
nodes.title: Why does a digital input need a pull-up or pull-down resistor
nodes.summary: Giving a floating input a defined state.

sections.heading: Why inputs float
sections.body: A digital input wired to nothing is "floating" — it picks up noise and reads randomly. A pull-up ties it to 5 V (reads HIGH until a switch pulls it LOW); a pull-down ties it to ground.

sections.heading: On the Arduino
sections.body: Skip the external resistor with pinMode(pin, INPUT_PULLUP), which enables the internal pull-up. The logic then inverts: a pressed/closed switch reads LOW.

nodes.hint: A switch that reads erratically when untouched is floating — enable INPUT_PULLUP (or add a 10 kΩ pull resistor) and invert your logic test.

nodes.name: Wheatstone Bridge
nodes.title: How does a Wheatstone bridge resolve a tiny resistance change
nodes.summary: Turning a small ΔR into a differential voltage.

sections.heading: The balanced bridge
sections.body: Four resistors in a diamond give zero differential output when R1/R2 = R4/R3. Replace one arm with a sensing element and a tiny resistance change unbalances the bridge, producing a small differential voltage proportional to that change.

sections.heading: Quarter, half, full
sections.body: Using one active arm (quarter), two (half), or all four (full) trades complexity for sensitivity and temperature compensation. The strain-gauge load cell is the canonical application.

nodes.hint: A bridge output of only a few millivolts buried in noise is expected — null the offset to ~0 V at rest first, then amplify with an op-amp stage before reading it.

nodes.name: Op-Amp Gain
nodes.title: How does an op-amp amplify a weak signal to a readable range
nodes.summary: Setting gain and respecting the rails.

sections.heading: Setting the gain
sections.body: A non-inverting amplifier has gain G = 1 + Rf/Rin; an inverting one has G = −Rf/Rin. This lifts millivolt bridge or sensor signals to a volt-level range the ADC can resolve.

sections.heading: Rails and offset
sections.body: A single-supply op-amp only outputs between its rails (0–5 V here), so centre your signal and watch for clipping. Input offset voltage gets amplified too — trim or reference it deliberately.

nodes.hint: An output stuck at a supply rail means the gain is too high for the input swing, or a DC offset is being amplified into saturation — reduce gain and bias the signal to re-centre it.

nodes.name: PWM & Duty Cycle
nodes.title: How does PWM fake an analog level with a square wave
nodes.summary: Duty cycle as an average voltage.

sections.heading: Duty cycle = average
sections.body: PWM switches a pin fully on/off fast; the fraction of time it is HIGH (duty cycle) sets the effective average voltage. analogWrite(pin, 0..255) maps to 0–100% duty, driving LED brightness, motor speed and heater power efficiently.

sections.heading: Frequency matters
sections.body: The right frequency depends on the load. A servo expects a specific ~50 Hz pulse train, not the default analogWrite frequency — which is why you use the Servo library to position it.

nodes.hint: A servo buzzing or refusing to hold position is getting the wrong PWM frequency — use the Servo library (correct ~50 Hz, 1–2 ms pulse) rather than analogWrite.

domains.title: Sensors
domains.blurb: How physical quantities become electrical signals.

nodes.name: Photoresistor (LDR)
nodes.title: What is a photoresistor and how do you read it
nodes.summary: Light-dependent resistance via a divider.

sections.heading: How it senses
sections.body: An LDR's resistance falls as light increases — from hundreds of kΩ in darkness to a few kΩ in bright light. Wired as one leg of a voltage divider, the divider output tracks brightness.

sections.heading: Reading it
sections.body: Feed the divider midpoint into an analog pin. A ~10 kΩ fixed resistor gives usable swing for room lighting. The response is nonlinear, so calibrate against the conditions you care about.

nodes.hint: If readings barely change between light and dark, the divider resistor is far from the LDR's working resistance — measure the LDR in your actual lighting and match it.

nodes.name: Thermistor (NTC)
nodes.title: What is an NTC thermistor and how do you convert it to °C
nodes.summary: A steeply nonlinear temperature resistor.

sections.heading: Negative coefficient
sections.body: An NTC thermistor's resistance drops as temperature rises. Like the LDR it is read through a voltage divider, but its resistance-vs-temperature curve is steep and strongly nonlinear.

sections.heading: Converting to °C
sections.body: Do not use a linear map. Apply the Beta-parameter equation or Steinhart-Hart with the datasheet coefficients to convert resistance to temperature accurately.

nodes.hint: Readings that look right at room temperature but drift badly when hot or cold mean a linear conversion — switch to the Beta equation with the part's datasheet constants.

nodes.name: Tilt Ball Switch
nodes.title: What is a tilt ball switch and how do you wire it
nodes.summary: An orientation-sensitive contact switch.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.body: A conductive ball rolls to bridge two contacts when tilted past a threshold, closing the circuit. It is effectively an orientation-sensitive switch — good for detecting flips, knocks or vibration.

sections.heading: Wiring
sections.body: Treat it like any momentary switch: it needs a pull resistor for a defined open state, and benefits from software debouncing because the rolling ball chatters.

nodes.hint: Multiple triggers per single tilt mean contact bounce — add INPUT_PULLUP and debounce in software (ignore changes within ~20–50 ms).

nodes.name: Strain Gauge / Load Cell
nodes.title: What is a strain gauge and how does it measure force
nodes.summary: Force as a tiny resistance change.

sections.heading: How it senses
sections.body: A bonded foil grid changes resistance slightly when stretched or compressed (its gauge factor relates ΔR/R to strain). Mounted on a flexure and wired into a Wheatstone bridge, four gauges form a load cell.

sections.heading: Conditioning the signal
sections.body: Bridge output is on the order of millivolts per volt of excitation, so it must be amplified — a dedicated 24-bit bridge ADC (HX711) or an op-amp instrumentation stage.

nodes.hint: A reading that drifts with no load change is usually thermal drift or a loose mount — use the opposite bridge arm for temperature compensation, tighten the fixture, and warm up before zeroing.

nodes.name: Ultrasonic (HC-SR04)
nodes.title: What is the HC-SR04 and how does time-of-flight give distance
nodes.summary: Distance from an echo round-trip.

sections.heading: Time of flight
sections.body: A 10 µs trigger pulse fires a burst of ultrasound; the echo pin then stays HIGH for the round-trip time. Distance is time × 343 / 2 (speed of sound, there and back).

sections.heading: Practical range
sections.body: Reliable from roughly 2 cm to 4 m, within a cone. Soft or angled surfaces scatter the echo. It is a 5 V part with separate trigger and echo pins.

nodes.hint: Distance that reads zero, max, or wildly unstable means a missed or scattered echo — aim at a flat hard surface within ~4 m, keep the trigger at ~10 µs, and add a timeout on pulseIn().

nodes.name: Soil Moisture
nodes.title: What is a capacitive soil moisture sensor and how is it calibrated
nodes.summary: Water content via dielectric constant.

sections.heading: Capacitive sensing
sections.body: It measures the dielectric constant of the surrounding soil, which rises with water content, and outputs an analog voltage. Capacitive probes avoid the electrode corrosion that plagues resistive sensors.

sections.heading: Calibration
sections.body: Raw readings are arbitrary, so record the value fully dry (in air) and fully wet (to the line in water) and map between them. Never submerge the electronics at the top of the board.

nodes.hint: A moisture percentage that makes no sense is uncalibrated — capture the dry-in-air and wet-in-water raw values, map() between them, and keep the circuitry out of the soil.

domains.title: Actuators & Output
domains.blurb: Turning signals back into motion and sound.

nodes.name: Active Buzzer
nodes.title: What is an active buzzer and how is it different from a passive one
nodes.summary: A self-oscillating audible alert.

sections.heading: Active vs passive
sections.body: An active buzzer contains its own oscillator — apply DC and it sounds at a fixed pitch. A passive buzzer is a tiny speaker that needs a driving frequency. For simple alerts the active type is just digitalWrite HIGH/LOW.

sections.heading: Driving it
sections.body: It is polarised, so orientation matters, and draws more than an LED — drive louder buzzers through a transistor rather than directly from a pin.

nodes.hint: An active buzzer that stays silent on a HIGH pin usually has reversed polarity — and if you need melodies, you actually need a passive buzzer driven with tone().

nodes.name: Servo Motor
nodes.title: What is a servo motor and how do pulses set its angle
nodes.summary: Angle from pulse width at ~50 Hz.

sections.heading: Position from pulses
sections.body: A hobby servo reads a ~50 Hz pulse train and moves its horn to an angle set by the pulse width (≈1 ms → 0°, ≈2 ms → 180°). Internal feedback holds that angle against load.

sections.heading: Driving it
sections.body: Use the Arduino Servo library, which generates the correct timing on a digital pin. Signal is logic-level; power should be separate.

nodes.hint: A servo that twitches or browns out the board on movement is drawing current spikes the 5 V rail cannot supply — power it from an external 5–6 V source with a common ground.

nodes.name: Stepper & Driver
nodes.title: What is a stepper motor, and why does it always need a driver
nodes.summary: Open-loop rotation in fixed steps.

sections.heading: Coils and drivers
sections.body: Steppers move in fixed steps by energising coil pairs in sequence. Never drive them from a pin — a driver (ULN2003 for the 28BYJ-48, or A4988/DRV8825 for bipolar NEMA motors) sequences the coils and limits current.

sections.heading: Identifying wiring
sections.body: Use a multimeter to find coil pairs (a pair shows continuity; across pairs is open) before connecting, so the step sequence energises the right windings.

nodes.hint: A motor that vibrates in place but will not rotate has its coil wiring/sequence wrong — buzz out the coil pairs with a multimeter and re-map the driver outputs.

nodes.name: Holding Torque
nodes.title: What is holding torque, and why do steppers skip steps
nodes.summary: The torque–speed limit of a stepper.

sections.heading: Discrete steps
sections.body: A stepper moves in fixed angular increments and can hold a position by energising its coils — that static resisting force is holding torque, giving open-loop positioning without an encoder.

sections.heading: Torque vs speed
sections.body: Available torque falls as step rate rises (the torque-speed curve). Push too fast or too hard and the rotor slips — it skips steps silently and loses position with no error reported.

nodes.hint: A motor that stutters or silently loses position under load is past the torque-speed curve — slow the step rate and/or raise the driver's current limit to recover holding torque.

nodes.name: Arduino Mega 2560
nodes.title: What is the Arduino Mega 2560 and what are its limits
nodes.summary: The central 5 V microcontroller board.

sections.heading: What it offers
sections.body: The Mega gives 54 digital I/O pins (15 PWM-capable), 16 analog inputs with a 10-bit ADC (0–1023), and multiple hardware serial ports. It is the hub every sensor and actuator connects to.

sections.heading: Logic levels
sections.body: It runs 5 V logic. Analog reads return 0–1023 across 0–5 V; digital writes are a clean 0 V / 5 V. Respect the ~20 mA per-pin limit and never back-power motors through the board.

nodes.hint: A board that resets or behaves randomly when a motor runs is being overdrawn — power actuators from a separate supply and tie the grounds together.

nodes.name: LMC6484 Op-Amp
nodes.title: What is the LMC6484, and why a rail-to-rail single-supply part
nodes.summary: A rail-to-rail CMOS quad op-amp.

sections.heading: Why this part
sections.body: The LMC6484 packs four CMOS op-amps with rail-to-rail input and output, running from a single supply — ideal for 5 V Arduino projects where signals live close to ground or the rail.

sections.heading: Using it well
sections.body: Add a decoupling capacitor near the supply pins, mind the pinout when wiring all four amplifiers, and remember the output still cannot quite reach the rails under load.

nodes.hint: An amplifier output that cannot reach the value you expect near 0 V or 5 V is losing headroom under load — lower the gain or bias the signal away from the rails.

nodes.name: Measuring Voltage
nodes.title: How do I measure voltage across a node with a multimeter
nodes.summary: Reading a powered node against ground.

sections.heading: Set up the meter
sections.body: Select DC volts, plug the black lead into COM and the red lead into the V/Ω jack. Voltage is measured in parallel — across a component or between a node and ground, with the circuit powered.

sections.heading: Take the reading
sections.body: Put the black probe on the common ground and the red probe on the node of interest. Start on a range above your expected value (or use autorange) and read once the value settles.

nodes.hint: A wildly wrong or negative voltage usually means the probes are on the wrong nodes or your ground reference is floating — re-confirm the black probe is on the same ground as the circuit.

nodes.name: Measuring Resistance
nodes.title: How do I measure resistance safely without damaging the meter
nodes.summary: Reading ohms on an unpowered part.

sections.heading: Power off first
sections.body: Resistance is measured on an unpowered circuit or an isolated component. Measuring a live circuit gives meaningless readings and can damage the meter. Set the dial to Ω.

sections.heading: Isolate the component
sections.body: For an accurate value, lift one leg of the component out of the circuit so parallel paths don't skew the reading. Use this to confirm resistor values and identify stepper coil pairs.

nodes.hint: A resistance reading lower than the marked value usually means another path is in parallel — lift one leg of the component out of the circuit and measure again.

nodes.name: Building a Divider
nodes.title: How do I build a sensor voltage divider on a breadboard
nodes.summary: Wiring a sensor + resistor to an analog pin.

sections.heading: The layout
sections.body: Run 5 V to one end, ground to the other, and place the sensor and fixed resistor in series between them. The junction between the two parts is your output — wire it to an analog pin such as A0.

sections.heading: Sanity check
sections.body: Before trusting code, measure the junction with a multimeter as you change the sensed quantity. The voltage should move smoothly between roughly 0 V and 5 V.

nodes.hint: If the analog pin reads flat, probe the divider junction directly — no movement there means a wiring break or a fixed resistor that swamps the sensor.

nodes.name: Wiring a Bridge
nodes.title: How do I wire and null a Wheatstone bridge before amplifying
nodes.summary: Balancing a bridge to ~0 V at rest.

sections.heading: Build and excite
sections.body: Wire the four arms into the diamond, apply a stable excitation voltage across one diagonal, and take the differential output from the other. With the active element at rest the output should sit near zero.

sections.heading: Null the offset
sections.body: Real resistors never match exactly, so trim one arm (or subtract the offset in software) until the resting output reads ~0 V. Only then does the amplified signal represent the change you care about.

nodes.hint: A bridge whose amplified output saturates immediately was never nulled — bring the resting differential to ~0 V before the gain stage, not after.

nodes.name: Calibrating Sensors
nodes.title: How do I calibrate an analog sensor to a real-world value
nodes.summary: Mapping raw counts to meaning.

sections.heading: Capture two anchors
sections.body: Record the raw ADC value at two known conditions — for a moisture probe, fully dry and fully wet; for an LDR, dark and bright. These anchor the range your sensor actually uses.

sections.heading: Map and threshold
sections.body: Use map() between the anchors to convert raw counts to a meaningful scale, and pick any control threshold from real measured readings rather than a guessed number.

nodes.hint: A sensor that reads "correct" indoors but fails in the real setting was calibrated against the wrong anchors — re-capture the extremes in the actual environment.

nodes.name: Power & Ground
nodes.title: How do I set up power rails and a common ground
nodes.summary: A shared reference for every part.

sections.heading: Shared reference
sections.body: Every measurement and signal is relative to ground. When a sensor, the Arduino, and an external supply all share a single common ground, voltages mean the same thing everywhere.

sections.heading: Separate supplies
sections.body: Motors and servos should draw from their own supply, but that supply's ground must still be tied to the Arduino ground — otherwise signals and readings drift unpredictably.

nodes.hint: Signals that drift once an external supply is added almost always mean the grounds were never tied together — bond every ground to one common rail.

nodes.name: Dataflow Paradigm
nodes.title: Why does LabVIEW not run top-to-bottom
nodes.summary: Execution by data availability.

sections.heading: Execution by data, not lines
sections.body: In a dataflow language a node executes the moment all its inputs are available — not in textual order. Independent branches run in parallel automatically, which is powerful but surprising if you think sequentially.

sections.heading: Forcing order
sections.body: When order matters (open port → read → close), you create artificial data dependencies — error clusters wired in series, or a Sequence structure — so one node cannot start until the previous finishes.

nodes.hint: A LabVIEW VI running its steps in the "wrong" order has no implied sequence — chain the error in/out wire through the nodes, or wrap them in a Flat Sequence, to force order.

nodes.name: LabVIEW Loops
nodes.title: How do I use loops and shift registers in LabVIEW
nodes.summary: Repeating logic and remembering state.

sections.heading: Front panel + block diagram
sections.body: Every VI has a front panel (the UI) and a block diagram (the graphical code). You build behaviour by wiring nodes; While and For loops repeat a section of diagram.

sections.heading: Shift registers
sections.body: A plain wire inside a loop resets every iteration. A shift register carries a value from one iteration to the next — essential for running totals, filters and state machines.

nodes.hint: A value that resets to its default every loop iteration was wired through a tunnel — right-click the loop border and Replace with Shift Register to persist it.

nodes.name: LabVIEW LINX
nodes.title: How do I drive Arduino pins from LabVIEW with LINX
nodes.summary: Controlling Arduino from the diagram.

sections.heading: What LINX does
sections.body: The LINX (Hobbyist) toolkit lets LabVIEW read and write Arduino pins directly — analog read, digital write, PWM — without writing C. Deploy its firmware once, then drive the board from the block diagram.

sections.heading: Session management
sections.body: Open the LINX session once before your main loop and close it once after — never inside the loop. Match the baud rate and select the correct COM port.

nodes.hint: LINX that runs slowly or errors repeatedly is opening/closing the session inside the loop — open before the loop, pass the reference through a shift register, close after.

nodes.name: LabVIEW VISA
nodes.title: How do I read an Arduino serial stream with VISA
nodes.summary: Parsing raw serial in LabVIEW.

sections.heading: When to use VISA
sections.body: When you write your own Arduino sketch that prints over Serial, VISA is how LabVIEW reads that stream. Configure the port (baud, data bits), then read/write bytes and parse them.

sections.heading: Framing the data
sections.body: Agree on a termination character (usually newline) on both sides so VISA knows where one message ends, and configure the serial read to stop on that terminator.

nodes.hint: VISA returning garbage, partial lines, or hanging is nearly always a baud-rate or termination-character mismatch — set both ends identical and clear the buffer before reading.

nodes.name: Threshold Control
nodes.title: How do I turn a sensor reading into an action on the Arduino
nodes.summary: analogRead → if/else → digitalWrite.

sections.heading: Read, compare, act
sections.body: In loop(), read the sensor with analogRead(), compare it to a threshold with an if/else, and command an actuator with digitalWrite(). This is the automatic-lighting pattern at the heart of the labs.

sections.heading: Choosing the threshold
sections.body: Set the threshold from calibrated measurements, and test around the boundary — not just obvious cases — so the actuator switches cleanly rather than chattering near the limit.

nodes.hint: An actuator that chatters on and off near the trigger point needs hysteresis — use two thresholds (one to turn on, a separate one to turn off) instead of a single value.

domains.blurb: Publishing sensor data to the cloud.

nodes.name: MQTT Protocol
nodes.title: What is MQTT and how does publish/subscribe work
nodes.summary: Broker-based lightweight messaging.

sections.heading: Publish / subscribe
sections.body: Devices do not talk directly. A publisher sends a message to a named topic on a central broker; any client subscribed to that topic receives it. This decouples your Arduino from the dashboard and scales to many devices.

sections.heading: Topics and QoS
sections.body: Topics are hierarchical strings (esi/3cc3/temp). Quality-of-Service levels trade delivery guarantees for overhead, and an auth token usually gates who may publish to a topic.

nodes.hint: Data that never reaches the cloud is usually a topic, token, or broker-address typo — check the exact (case-sensitive) topic string first, then the credentials, then the broker host/port.

nodes.name: ThingsBoard Cloud
nodes.title: How do I exchange LabVIEW data with ThingsBoard Cloud
nodes.summary: Publish JSON telemetry, receive persistent shared attributes, and build a device dashboard.

sections.heading: One cloud device per physical project
sections.body: ThingsBoard stores measurements as telemetry and persistent cloud-to-device settings as shared attributes. Build gauges, time-series charts, indicators, and controls around the same device entity.

sections.heading: MQTT connection and topics
sections.body: Connect to mqtt.thingsboard.cloud on port 1883 with the device access token as the username and a blank password. Publish JSON to v1/devices/me/telemetry and exchange desired-state values through the ThingsBoard attribute topics.

nodes.hint: An empty widget means a token, label, or rate-limit problem — verify the token is the device token (not the account token), the variable label matches exactly, and you are under the free-tier limit.
